planting.note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; LSU Tiger was developed by the LSU AgCenter fig breeding program specifically for Gulf Coast disease pressure and humidity, and shares the program's characteristic split- and souring-resistance.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; like its LSU AgCenter sibling releases, LSU Tiger fig was bred specifically to perform reliably in the humid, disease-prone conditions of the Gulf Coast and Deep South. Its most distinctive feature is its striking immature fruit — young, unripe figs are boldly striped in yellow-green and dark green, giving the variety its 'Tiger' name — before ripening to a bronze-brown skin with sweet, richly flavored, amber-to-strawberry-colored flesh. The variety carries useful resistance to fruit splitting and souring, common problems for figs grown where summer rains fall during ripening, and its ornamental striped immature fruit makes it a conversation piece in the garden even before harvest. A good choice for Gulf South growers who want the LSU program's disease resistance along with a visually distinctive fruit, zone 7–11.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Fig Variety Trials

planting.note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; Flanders is notably more cold-hardy than most fig cultivars, tolerating winter dieback and regrowing reliably from the crown even after a hard freeze, making it a good choice at the cooler edge of fig-growing range.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the more cold-hardy fig cultivars available, reliably resprouting from the roots after winters that kill back the top growth of less hardy varieties. Flanders is an old Belgian fig cultivar long grown in home gardens and small orchards for its dependable production of medium, brown-skinned figs with sweet, amber flesh and good flavor, and for its resilience in marginal fig-growing climates where winter cold is a limiting factor. It typically produces a modest breba (early summer) crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, and the fruit holds reasonably well against splitting in humid weather. Its cold tolerance makes it a valuable choice for gardeners at the northern edge of the fig range, or in a Gulf South garden where an occasional hard freeze is a risk, zone 6–10.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Fig Fact Sheet

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, in a site sheltered from north wind; Changsha is among the most cold-hardy true mandarins available, tolerating brief drops into the low teens (°F) once mature, though young trees still need winter protection for the first several years.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, sheltered from cold north winds; mulch well and protect young trees through their first few winters until established. Changsha is a small-fruited mandarin native to Hunan Province, China, valued above nearly all other citrus for its exceptional cold hardiness — mature trees have survived and fruited after temperatures well below 10°F, making it one of the few true mandarins that can be grown outdoors, unprotected, in the Gulf South and even into the coastal Southeast beyond typical citrus range. The small, flattened, deep orange fruits are intensely sweet with a rich, aromatic mandarin flavor, though they are notably seedy, which has historically limited commercial interest despite the outstanding flavor and hardiness. Changsha is widely used by cold-hardy citrus breeders and hobbyists both as a garden fruit tree in its own right and as breeding stock for hardier hybrid mandarins. A rewarding choice for Gulf South gardeners who want the flavor of a true mandarin from a tree that can survive outdoors through a hard winter, zone 8–10.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Citrus for the Home Garden
University of Georgia Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Thomasville citrangequat is among the most cold-hardy edible citrus hybrids available, with mature wood tolerating temperatures down to near 0°F, making it plantable well outside the range of standard citrus in the Gulf South and Southeast.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a fruiting citrus, tolerating hard freezes that would kill standard citrus outright, though a sheltered microclimate still improves fruit set and tree vigor. Thomasville citrangequat is a three-way citrus hybrid — a cross of citrange (trifoliate orange × sweet orange) with kumquat — developed by USDA citrus breeder Dr. Walter Swingle in Thomasville, Georgia in the early 20th century specifically to push the boundary of cold-hardy edible citrus northward out of Florida. The small, oval, orange-yellow fruits have an aromatic, tart-sweet, marmalade-quality flavor with edible skin in the kumquat tradition, best used for marmalade, candying, or juice rather than fresh peeling and eating. The tree also carries attractive small trifoliate-influenced leaves and light thorns, and its extreme hardiness has made it a mainstay of cold-hardy citrus hobbyist plantings from the Gulf Coast through the Southeast. A rewarding novelty citrus for growers pushing the cold edge of the citrus range, zone 7–10.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Citrus for the Home Garden

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Ichang lemon is one of the most cold-hardy citrus species, with mature wood tolerating temperatures down to around 0°F, and is often grown as much for its hardiness and rootstock value as for its tart fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the hardiest citrus species available, surviving winter conditions that kill standard lemons and limes outright. Citrus ichangensis (Ichang lemon, or Ichang papeda) is a wild citrus species native to the mountainous borderlands of China, prized by cold-hardy citrus breeders and enthusiasts as one of the parents behind many of today's cold-tolerant citrus hybrids, thanks to its unusual combination of true citrus flavor and genuine winter hardiness. The rough-skinned, lemon-like fruit is highly acidic and aromatic with a distinct floral note, used much like a true lemon for juice, zest, and flavoring rather than fresh eating out of hand. Its glossy, deep green, notably large-winged leaves and modest thorns give it strong ornamental value even apart from fruiting. A rewarding choice for gardeners in the Gulf South and Southeast who want to grow citrus outside the usual protected range, and a useful parent plant for anyone interested in breeding hardier citrus hybrids, zone 7–10.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm
